query: Context: our lab in Provo, Utah (about 1,400 m elevation) makes and stores aluminum-alloy powders for additive-manufacturing research. A walk-in enclosure inside the lab is supplied with air from a refrigerant (compressor) dehumidifier and exhausted continuously to building exhaust. The surrounding room sits at 21.7-22.2 C and 35-60% relative humidity (RH), dew point 6-13 C, tracking outdoor humidity. On the first night with the dehumidifier on, air inside the enclosure was 24 C at 35-42% RH (dew point 8-10 C) while the room was expected at about 22 C and 56% RH (dew point about 13 C); a hand-held reading showed about 27 C (80 F) at about 30% RH. So the compressor heat raises the enclosure temperature by roughly 2-5 C while the dehumidifier removes about 15-30% of the water vapor. Powders stored there, in sealed containers with silica-gel packets inside chemical storage cabinets, include gas-atomized AlSi10Mg (15-45 um, from MSE Supplies), silicon powder (98-99.5% Si), stainless-steel powder, and soon ultrasonically atomized aluminum alloys containing Mg, Cu, Zn, Li, Sc, Zr, Ce and Er, made in an argon-purged atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder). Question: what do published powder-storage, powder-ageing and powder-reuse studies on laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (and other aluminum AM powders such as AlSi7Mg, Scalmalloy, Al-Cu and Al-Ce alloys) report about oxygen pickup, moisture or hydrogen pickup, flowability (Hall flow, avalanche angle, cohesion) and hydrogen porosity in printed parts after storage at controlled temperature and humidity? Report conditions (temperature, RH, container, duration), measured changes with numbers, and DOIs. Which drying procedures (temperature, time, vacuum) were shown to restore the powder? What storage temperature and RH do aluminum AM powder suppliers (e.g., Valimet, Carpenter Additive, IMR Metal Powder Technologies, ECKART, Oerlikon, EOS, SLM Solutions) and standards or guides (ASTM F3049, ISO/ASTM 52907, ASTM F3318, ASTM F3571 or others) recommend? Finally, what is known about the risks introduced by temperature differences and cycling during storage: condensation when a container stored in a cooler place is opened in warmer humid air or vice versa, pressure-driven air exchange ('breathing') of imperfectly sealed containers, and the reduced water capacity of silica gel at higher temperature? Could silica gel or its dust contaminate aluminum powders stored with it? Give quantitative values with DOIs, and say explicitly where evidence is lacking.

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

question.description: Specific question to gather evidence for.
question.title: Question

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding
search will be performed on underlying content to find most relevant texts.
text_name_focus_list.title: Text Name Focus List

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)
query.title: Query

after.description:
Minimum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20150101' for patents after Jan 1, 2015.
after.title: After

before.description:
Maximum patent date. Format: YYYYMMDD.
Example: '20200101' for patents before Jan 1, 2020.
before.title: Before

date_type.description:
Type of date that after and before refer to. Must be either 'publication'
or 'filing'. Only necessary to set if after and/or before are set.
date_type.title: Date Type

inventor.description: Filter by inventor name(s). Comma-separated for multiple.
inventor.title: Inventor

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.
plan_json.title: Plan Json

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening
        - HEALTH_SERVICES_RESEARCH: Health Services Research

info.name: collect_cited_papers_in_evidence
info.description:
Collect papers by traversing the citations of relevant papers to increase the paper count.

This tool has no effect if called when paper count or relevant papers are zero.
This tool will find papers that are likely to lead to more relevant evidence.
The papers found have a higher chance of relevance because this tool starts from relevant evidence.
This tool's usefulness increases with the amount of gathered evidence as there's more citations to consider.

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

text_name_list.description:
A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.
text_name_list.title: Text Name List

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context: our lab in Provo, Utah (about 1,400 m elevation) makes and stores aluminum-alloy powders for additive-manufacturing research. A walk-in enclosure inside the lab is supplied with air from a refrigerant (compressor) dehumidifier and exhausted continuously to building exhaust. The surrounding room sits at 21.7-22.2 C and 35-60% relative humidity (RH), dew point 6-13 C, tracking outdoor humidity. Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Powder feedstock is the primary input to metal additive manufacturing processes such as laser powder bed fusion. Its characteristics are crucial for producing high-quality components. Realization of the waste reduction and cost benefits that this technology offers requires reclaiming, processing, and reusing powder feedstock. While these benefits can be significant, there are challenges related to the industrial implementation of powder reuse, including the variability in powder quality that can propagate through to the produced material. This variability can be both negative and positive, but ultimately leads to uncertainty for both users and regulators. This means material and process qualifications are difficult to achieve when powder feedstock is being repeatedly reused. This study reports the effects of 175 Ti-6Al-4V ELI powder reuse cycles, characterized at 23, 104, and 175 reuses, in a certified medical device production facility, whereby powder was topped up with virgin powder from the same production lot after each build cycle. To the best of our knowledge, this is the longest reuse campaign reported in the literature. During this campaign, flowability improved with Hall flow rate decreasing by 5.4% and apparent density increasing by 0.8%. The particle size distribution remained stable, with net changes of no more than 2.1%. Particle elongation decreased by 2.9%, and the form factor distribution narrowed around its unchanged mean. Oxygen concentration progressively increased in both the powder (8.2%) and the produced material (25.1%). The average microhardness increased by 3.7% at all measured indentation depths, which is attributed to this oxygen pickup. All property means remained within the material specification limits for both powder and produced material throughout the reuse campaign. The findings of this study suggest that such extensive reuse campaigns can be implemented while fulfilling the requirements of industry powder material specifications, although such reuse processes do induce variability in the properties of both the powder and produced material. The degree of this variability is specific to the type of powder reuse approach implemented and the specific characteristics of the associated powder processing environments.</jats:p>

In this paper, the capability of laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) systems to process stainless steel alloys is reviewed. Several classes of stainless steels are analyzed (i.e., austenitic, martensitic, precipitation hardening and duplex), showing the possibility of satisfactorily processing this class of materials and suggesting an enlargement of the list of alloys that can be manufactured, targeting different applications. Micro surface roughness typical of the as-built material can act as a crack initiator, reducing the strength in both quasi-static and dynamic conditions.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) has attracted significant attention in both the industry and academic fields since its inception, providing unprecedented advantages to fabricate complex-shaped metallic components. The printing quality and performance of L-PBF alloys are influenced by numerous variables consisting of feedstock powders, manufacturing process, and post-treatment. As the starting materials, metallic powders play a critical role in influencing the fabrication cost, printing consistency, and properties. Given their deterministic roles, the present review aims to retrospect the recent progress on metallic powders for L-PBF including characterization, preparation, and reuse. The powder characterization mainly serves for printing consistency while powder preparation and reuse are introduced to reduce the fabrication costs. Various powder characterization and preparation methods are presented in the beginning by analyzing the measurement principles, advantages, and limitations. Subsequently, the effect of powder reuse on the powder characteristics and mechanical performance of L-PBF parts is analyzed, focusing on steels, nickel-based superalloys, titanium and titanium alloys, and aluminum alloys. The evolution trends of powders and L-PBF parts vary depending on specific alloy systems, which makes the proposal of a unified reuse protocol infeasible. Finally, perspectives are presented to cater to the increased applications of L-PBF technologies for future investigations. The present state-of-the-art work can pave the way for the broad industrial applications of L-PBF by enhancing printing consistency and reducing the total costs from the perspective of powders.

Abstract:
In powder bed fusion additive manufacturing, the powder feedstock quality is of paramount importance; as the process relies on thin layers of powder being spread and selectively melted to manufacture 3D metallic components. Conventional powder quality assessments for additive manufacturing are limited to particle morphology, particle size distribution, apparent density and flowability. However, recent studies are highlighting that these techniques may not be the most appropriate. The problem is exacerbated when studying aluminium powders as their complex cohesive behaviors dictate their flowability. The current study compares the properties of three different AlSi7Mg powders, and aims to obtain insights about the minimum required properties for acceptable powder feedstock. In addition to conventional powder characterization assessments, the powder spread density, moisture sorption, surface energy, work of cohesion, and powder rheology, were studied. This work has shown that the presence of fine particles intensifies the pick-up of moisture increasing the total particle surface energy as well as the inter-particle cohesion. This effect hinders powder flow and hence, the spreading of uniform layers needed for optimum printing. When spherical particles larger than 48 µm with a narrow particle distribution are present, the moisture sorption as well as the surface energy and cohesion characteristics are decreased enhancing powder spreadability. This result suggest that by manipulating particle distribution, size and morphology, challenging powder feedstock such as Al, can be optimized for powder bed fusion additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
The most widely used metal additive manufacturing processes utilize powder that is spread or fed onto a building platform. Although there are reviews of the literature on some aspects of the powder, many aspects have been un-der-reviewed or unreviewed. The present work is a review of the literature on these aspects. Articles published in the open literature through the end of February 2022 were collected by consulting highly regarded relevant biblio-graphic databases, such as Google Scholar and Science Direct. The aspects reviewed were emerging methods of powder production, methods used to improve the quality of a powder after production by a well-established method, influence of variables of well-established powder production methods on powder properties, influence of powder production method on powder properties, and influence of powder reuse on properties of powders of a wide collection of alloys. One key finding was that with regard to powder reuse, the only consistent finding is that it leads to increase in the oxygen content of the powder. Another key finding was that the literature on the aspects of the literature reviewed herein contains many shortcomings and gaps, which suggest potential areas for future research, such as techniques for optimization of process variables for a given combination of metal powder and powder production method and development of methods for production of powders of new/emerging metallic materials.

Abstract:
In aeronautics, additive manufacturing (AM) leads to specific benefits, mainly connected to topological optimization for weight reduction, the decrease in “buy-to-fly” ratio, and the operations of maintenance, repair, and overhaul. Al alloys processed by AM technologies are extensively investigated and play an increasing role in the production of aircraft structural parts. Based on the recent literature and research activity of the authors, this work examines advantages and drawbacks involved in the printing of Al alloys. Abstract:
Complex structures can now be manufactured easily utilizing AM technologies to meet the pre-requisite objectives such as reduced part numbers, greater functionality, and lightweight, among others. Polymers, metals, and ceramics are the few materials that can be used in AM technology, but metallic materials (Magnesium and Aluminum) are attracting more attention from the research and industrial point of view. Understanding the role processing parameters of laser-based additive manufacturing is critical to maximize the usage of material in forming the product geometry. LPBF (Laser powder-based fusion) method is regarded as a potent and effective additive manufacturing technique for creating intricate 3D forms/parts with high levels of precision and reproducibility together with acceptable metallurgical characteristics. While dealing with LBPF, some degree of porosity is acceptable because it is unavoidable; hot ripping and cracking must be avoided, though. The necessary manufacturing of pre-alloyed powder and ductility remains to be the primary concern while dealing with a laser-based additive manufacturing approach. The presence of the Al-Si eutectic phase in AlSi10Mg and AlSi12 alloy attributing to excellent castability and low shrinkage, attaining the most attention in the laser-based approach. Related studies with these alloys along with precipitation hardening and heat treatment processing were discussed. The Pure Mg, Mg-Al alloy, Mg-RE alloy, and Mg-Zn alloy along with the mechanical characteristics, electrochemical durability, and biocompatibility of Mg-based material have been elaborated in the work-study. The review article also summarizes the processing parameters of the additive manufacturing powder-based approach relating to different Mg-based alloys. For future aspects, the optimization of processing parameters, composition of the alloy, and quality of powder material used will significantly improve the ductility of additively manufactured Mg alloy by the LPBF approach. Other than that, the recycling of Mg-alloy powder hasn’t been investigated yet. Meanwhile, the post-processing approach, including a homogeneous coating on the porous scaffolds, will mark the suitability in terms of future advancements in Mg and Al-based alloys.

Abstract:
Metal powder-based additive manufacturing (AM) relies on consistently successful processing of feedstock powder, necessitating through-process predictability in powder properties and behavior. However, routine powder handling and storage may degrade powder performance by influencing flowability and moisture content through exposure to ambient conditions. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effects of repeated environmental exposure on the flowability and moisture content of Al 5056 and Ta powders for AM applications. Using Carney Funnel flow tests, thermogravimetric analysis, and particle size/shape analysis, powder characterization helped elucidate powder property and behavioral changes with exposure. Results indicated inconsistent flowability and moisture content changes for both material types when exposure conditions were altered. Correlational statistics highlighted the most influential particle characteristics on powder behavior after exposure; particle morphology was most impactful for the semi-spherical Al 5056, whereas moisture content and particle size were most significant for the angular Ta. While exposure to laboratory conditions minimally changed powder performance in this study, caution is advised when handling and storing powders in more “extreme” environments. Powder users are urged to implement quality controls alongside powder characterization to pinpoint how specific powders should be treated, handled, and stored in a given environment for successful processing in AM.

Abstract:
In this work, we study three aluminum oxides (alpha, gamma, boehmite) and various oxidized metallic aluminum powders to observe their dehydration and decomposition behavior using in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). We find that a temperature increase to the aluminum oxides (aluminas) reduces physically adsorbed water molecules to reveal the presence of hydroxyl groups. All three aluminas contained bridged hydroxyls located at 3670 cm−1; we found additional surface hydroxyls, which varied based on the oxidation state of the aluminum atom. Oxidized metallic aluminum powders that were aged resulted in similar behavior; however, the results differed depending on the method of aging. We find that naturally aged aluminum (NA-Al) powders with heavy oxidation in the form of the tri-hydroxide decomposed and did not reveal any detectable surface hydroxyl peaks. When aged using artificial methods (AA-Al), we find both surface hydroxyls, including bridged hydroxyls at 3670, 3700, and 3730 cm−1, and a remaining boehmite-like surface. These results show that metallic aluminum powders can be tailored for specific applications, regardless of age. It also elucidates different ways to pre-process the powders to control the surface oxide layer, corroborated by comparison with the models oxides studied herein.

### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Study (authors, year, DOI) | Alloy | Storage condition (temperature, RH, container, duration) | Measured change (O, H₂O, H) | Change in flowability | Change in printed-part porosity | Additional notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fedina et al. (2022), [10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024) | AlSi10Mg; virgin and once-processed/recycled (“R0”) powder | Thermal aging in a muffle furnace for 96 h; exact temperature, RH, and container atmosphere are not available in the extracted evidence. This is accelerated thermal aging, not controlled-humidity storage. | Virgin: O **0.067 → 0.257 wt%** after aging; R0: **0.072 → 0.274 wt%**. H remained **0.003 wt%** in virgin/aged powder and changed **0.003 → 0.004 wt%** for R0/R0-aged powder; therefore no clear hydrogen-pickup trend. N changed from **<0.005 to <0.010 wt%**. Moisture was not quantified. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000020) | No Hall/Carney flow, avalanche-angle, or cohesion values reported in the extracted evidence. D50 changed from **39.8 μm** (virgin) and **39.9 μm** (R0) to **43.5 μm** after aging; laser absorbance fell approximately **15%**. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004) | Reported total porosity increased from **3.16%** for virgin-powder parts to **6.5%** for aged-powder parts. The pores were associated with oxidation, reduced wetting/absorbance, and lack of fusion—not demonstrated to be hydrogen pores. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000019) | Strong evidence for persistent oxygen/oxide pickup; weak evidence for H pickup. LPBF used Ar with chamber O₂ **<1000 ppm**. Drying may remove physically adsorbed water but not the added oxide oxygen. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020) |
| Peres et al. (2024), [10.1590/1980-5373-mr-2023-0490](https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-5373-mr-2023-0490) | AlSi10Mg | Five-day exposures included **50°C/17% RH**, **50°C/60% RH**, **23°C/29% RH** (silica gel), and **23°C/90% RH**; sealed furnace/box arrangements were used. Initial laboratory condition was about **19.5°C/75% RH**. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000018) | Moisture was measured by Karl Fischer vaporization (method stated suitable above **25 ppm**), but numerical before/after water contents are unavailable in the extracted evidence. O and H were not quantitatively measured. High humidity repeatedly produced agglomerates and oxidation-related spectral changes. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000007) | Carney funnel, 50-g samples, five replicates: storage generally increased flow time. **50°C/17% RH maintained the newly opened powder’s flow behavior**; high humidity produced agglomeration and poorer flow. Numerical flow times were not available. Apparent density stayed near **1.37 g/cm³**. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014) | Parts were not printed; no porosity measurement. The authors inferred that retained moisture/agglomerates could promote LPBF porosity, but did not quantify that link. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000022) | Supports humidity control more strongly than elevated temperature alone. The low-RH treatments demonstrated preservation, not proven restoration of already degraded powder. |
| Cordova, Campos & Tinga (2017), DOI not available in extracted source | AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy; comparison with Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 | Moist aging: **50°C/80% RH for 72 h** in a climate chamber. Comparison treatments: vacuum drying at **85°C for 6 h** and air drying at **150°C for 20 min**; vacuum pressure was not reported. (pqac-00000013) | AlSi10Mg had the largest qualitative moisture increase and developed visibly different layers after humid aging. Moisture was assessed by loss on drying at **150°C for 20 min**, but readable numerical water contents are unavailable. O and H were not measured. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000016) | Hall funnel, **50 g**: AlSi10Mg flow improved after vacuum drying but, after 50°C/80% RH exposure, **did not flow**. Scalmalloy was also difficult or unable to flow after moisturizing and, anomalously, after vacuum drying. Exact times were unavailable. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000017) | No printed-part porosity measurements. | Directly demonstrates high humidity’s severe effect on Al alloy flow and qualitative recovery of AlSi10Mg by vacuum drying, but not complete quantitative restoration; vacuum level was omitted. |
| Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018), [10.3390/ma11122386](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma11122386) | Three AlSi7Mg powders (A, B, C) differing in size and morphology | Powders were oven-dried and then repeatedly tested in air at **40% RH**; storage container and long-term exposure duration were not reported. This was an environmental/repeated-flow experiment rather than a long-duration storage trial. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | Moisture pickup was not reported as ppm or wt%. Fine, irregular powder C adsorbed more water and showed stronger agglomeration/cohesion than coarser spherical A and B. O and H were not measured. | Baseline Hall flow: A **33.0 ± 0.4 s/50 g**, B **32.7 ± 0.7 s/50 g**, C **did not flow**. Carney flow: A and B **6.1 ± 0.1 s/50 g**; C **15.3 ± 0.4 s/50 g**. During 40% RH repeated testing, A/B remained near **6 s**; C worsened from **16 to ~22 s** within 5 min after oven removal, then improved to **14 s** after 30 measurements, attributed to shear breakup of agglomerates. Static repose angles: A **30 ± 4°**, B **26 ± 3°**, C **39 ± 4°**; C’s dynamic angle was about **38° at 2–6 rpm** and its cohesion index ranked highest. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | No parts were printed for a storage-to-porosity comparison. | Shows that fine-particle content and morphology strongly mediate humidity sensitivity; it does not isolate storage age or quantify chemical pickup. |
| Da Silva et al. (2022), [10.1016/j.matdes.2022.110677](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2022.110677) | AlSi10Mg used in directed-energy deposition (DED), not LPBF | Powder was aged under several conditions, but temperature, RH, container, and duration are unavailable in the extracted evidence. | Aging increased both O and H, but numerical concentrations are unavailable here. Particle size and morphology changed little. (pqac-00000021) | Conventional powder-flow values were not reported. Oxidation reduced laser absorbance and changed melt wetting and deposited-track geometry. | Aged-powder deposits had **3.5–4.2×** the porosity of deposits from unaged powder; authors attributed this mainly to hydrogen pores from higher feedstock H. Yield strength fell **19.0%**, UTS **14.2%**, and elongation increased **99.2%**. (pqac-00000021) | Strong evidence linking aged AlSi10Mg powder to hydrogen porosity, but it is DED evidence and lacks extractable controlled-storage parameters; it should not be treated as a quantitative LPBF storage limit. |
| Grubbs, Sousa & Cote (2022), [10.3390/met12040603](https://doi.org/10.3390/met12040603) | Semi-spherical Al 5056; Ta comparator | Repeated laboratory environmental exposure; exact temperature, RH, containers, and exposure schedule are not present in the extracted evidence. | TGA loss-on-drying changes were inconsistent; numerical Al 5056 moisture, O, and H changes are unavailable. | Carney-flow changes were inconsistent and generally small under the tested laboratory exposures. For Al 5056, morphology affected behavior more strongly than measured moisture. No Hall-flow, avalanche-angle, or cohesion values are available. (pqac-00000012) | No printed-part porosity assessment. | Indicates that ordinary laboratory exposure need not measurably degrade every Al powder; results cannot be generalized to finer spherical AlSi10Mg or more humid environments. |
| Tonelli et al. (2020), [10.1007/s00170-019-04641-x](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-019-04641-x) | Gas-atomized A357 (AlSi7Mg-type) powders L and H | Atmospheric muffle-furnace drying: **60°C for 3 h** or **200°C for 1 h**, ramp **100°C/h**, followed by air cooling. Initial storage RH/container and vacuum were not specified. | Adsorbed moisture was blamed for poor as-received flow, but numerical water, oxygen, and hydrogen contents before/after drying were not reported in the extracted evidence. | Supplier baseline: powder L tended not to flow; powder H Carney flow was **38.25 s/75 g**. Post-drying flow values were not available, so the magnitude of restoration cannot be quantified. (pqac-00000015) | SLM specimens were produced and assessed after drying, but no storage-linked or hydrogen-specific porosity change is available in the extracted evidence. | Establishes practicable atmospheric drying schedules for a related Al alloy, but does not prove which schedule best restored flow or whether 200°C altered surface chemistry. |

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "blockquote", "description": "Summary on risks introduced by temperature differences and thermal cycling during storage of aluminum AM powders: condensation when containers are opened in humid/warmer air (or vice versa), pressure-driven air exchange ('breathing'), and the reduced water capacity of silica gel at higher temperature; potential for silica gel or its dust to contaminate stored powders. Include quantitative or explicit evidence where found, and indicate evidence gaps."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

> **Condensation threshold.** Condensation is controlled by **dew point, not RH alone**. With room air at a dew point near **13°C**, any powder, container, or lid surface below about **13°C** can acquire liquid water when opened there. Enclosure air with an **8–10°C dew point** would require a surface below **8–10°C** for condensation. Therefore, powder equilibrated at **22–27°C** will not condense water merely because it is moved between the stated room and enclosure; the significant case is a container arriving from storage or transport below the receiving-air dew point. Guidance to keep powder and container under the same environmental conditions is consistent with minimizing condensation during transfer. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026)
>
> **Warm-to-cool transfer.** Opening a warm container in cooler air does not ordinarily condense water on the still-warm powder. Risk appears later if humid replacement air is admitted and the closed container subsequently cools below that air’s dew point. Thus, acclimatization should occur while the container remains sealed, followed by opening only after container temperature exceeds the local dew point with a safety margin.
>
> **Pressure-driven “breathing.”** For a rigid headspace containing ideal gas, heating from **22°C to 27°C** raises absolute pressure by approximately **27/295 = 1.7%** if perfectly sealed—about **1.4 kPa** at Provo’s approximate **85 kPa** atmospheric pressure. An imperfect seal may vent roughly this order of headspace volume while warming and draw humid room air back while cooling; repeated cycles can progressively defeat an argon purge or desiccant. The actual exchanged fraction depends strongly on seal leakage, headspace, heating rate, and lid compliance. **No retrieved aluminum-AM study directly measured breathing rates, oxygen/water ingress, or powder degradation under 2–5°C storage cycles.** Standards-oriented guidance instead favors stable conditions, inert gas for oxidation-prone powders, and temperature/RH/O₂ monitoring. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026)
>
> **Why small cycles still matter.** At constant water-vapor content, cooling raises RH; warming lowers RH but does not by itself remove water from a closed container. Consequently, the enclosure’s lower displayed RH partly reflects its **2–5°C higher temperature**, while its lower dew point demonstrates that the dehumidifier also removes water. Published AlSi10Mg conditioning studies show severe flow degradation at **50°C/80% RH for 72 h**—including failure to flow—and recurrent agglomeration at high RH, but they do not establish a harmless threshold for repeated modest thermal cycles. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013)
>
> **Silica-gel temperature effect.** Silica gel’s equilibrium water loading generally decreases as temperature rises, so warming can reduce its remaining adsorption capacity and can desorb part of previously held water into a closed headspace. Cooling reverses the equilibrium but may temporarily expose powder to higher RH. **The retrieved sources provide no quantitative silica-gel isotherm, packet-sizing rule, or measured capacity at 22 versus 27°C**, so a numerical capacity penalty for this enclosure cannot be supported here. The relevant AlSi10Mg experiment used silica gel to obtain approximately **23°C/29% RH**, but did not quantify gel loading, lifetime, or higher-temperature capacity. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000018)
>
> **Possible contamination from packets.** Intact, low-dusting, vapor-permeable packets kept physically separate from powder present little direct-transfer opportunity. A torn packet, friable granules, or dusty packet exterior could introduce silica particles or indicator chemicals; these foreign particles could alter flow, chemistry, or inclusion populations. **No retrieved LPBF aluminum study demonstrated silica-gel dust contamination, quantified a tolerable silica concentration, or linked packet use to printed-part defects.** Therefore, contamination is plausible but presently unquantified; loose desiccant should not contact powder, packets should be inspected and restrained outside the powder bed, and indicating gels containing cobalt salts should be avoided where chemical purity matters.
>
> **Practical implication for this laboratory.** The reported enclosure condition is not intrinsically a condensation hazard for powder already near room temperature, and its **8–10°C dew point** is better than the room’s approximately **13°C** dew point. The more defensible controls are stable temperature, genuinely airtight containers with minimal headspace, sealed acclimatization before opening, dew-point logging, protected/non-dusting desiccant, and periodic moisture, oxygen, and flow testing rather than reliance on cabinet RH alone. General guidance cited in the retrieved record recommends approximately **15–25°C and <55% RH**, inert handling for reactive powders, and rechecking oxygen, moisture, and flow after extended storage; however, the provenance of those numerical limits should be verified against the current full standard before treating them as normative requirements. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026)


*Blockquote: Quantitative screening of condensation and container-breathing risks for the reported Provo conditions, together with the evidence limits concerning silica-gel capacity and contamination.*

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

text_name_focus_list.description:
if there are known text names that are relevant to the question,
you can specify them here. This will ensure that the tool will look at these text names
first, and then look at the rest of the evidence. If left as `None`, an embedding

Only repeat a maximum of three times.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan for to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string representing the plan. It should be a dictionary
with top-level key "objectives", whose value is a list of objectives.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,
    one of: pending, in-progress, or completed.
    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

Field Reference:
    High Priority Fields (weight >= 0.8):
        - NCTId (1.0): Trial identifier
        - Acronym (1.0): Study acronym
        - BriefTitle (0.89): Short title
        - OfficialTitle (0.85): Full official title
        - Condition (0.81): Medical condition
        - InterventionName (0.8): Primary intervention name
        - OverallStatus: Trial status

    Medium Priority Fields (0.5-0.79):
        - InterventionOtherName (0.75): Alternative intervention names
        - Phase (0.65): Trial phase
        - StdAge (0.65): Standard age groups
        - Keyword (0.6): Study keywords
        - BriefSummary (0.6): Short description
        - SecondaryOutcomeMeasure (0.5): Secondary outcomes

    Low Priority Fields (< 0.5):
        - DesignPrimaryPurpose (0.3): Primary purpose of study
        - StudyType (0.3)
        - Various descriptive, location, and administrative fields

Supported Enums:
    Phase:
        - EARLY_PHASE1: Early Phase 1
        - PHASE1: Phase 1
        - PHASE2: Phase 2
        - PHASE3: Phase 3
        - PHASE4: Phase 4
        - NA: Not Applicable

    StandardAge:
        - CHILD: Child
        - ADULT: Adult
        - OLDER_ADULT: Older Adult

    Status:
        - RECRUITING: Currently recruiting participants
        - ACTIVE_NOT_RECRUITING: Active but not recruiting
        - COMPLETED: Study completed
        - ENROLLING_BY_INVITATION: Enrolling by invitation only
        - NOT_YET_RECRUITING: Not yet recruiting
        - SUSPENDED: Study suspended
        - TERMINATED: Study terminated
        - WITHDRAWN: Study withdrawn
        - AVAILABLE: Available
        - NO_LONGER_AVAILABLE: No longer available
        - TEMPORARILY_NOT_AVAILABLE: Temporarily not available
        - APPROVED_FOR_MARKETING: Approved for marketing
        - WITHHELD: Withheld
        - UNKNOWN: Unknown status

    StudyType:
        - INTERVENTIONAL: Interventional studies
        - OBSERVATIONAL: Observational studies
        - EXPANDED_ACCESS: Expanded access studies

    PrimaryPurpose:
        - TREATMENT: Treatment
        - PREVENTION: Prevention
        - DIAGNOSTIC: Diagnostic
        - ECT: Educational/Counseling/Training
        - SUPPORTIVE_CARE: Supportive Care
        - SCREENING: Screening

Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,

This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

answer.description: valid answer, cited with citation IDs.
answer.title: Answer

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: Context: our lab in Provo, Utah (about 1,400 m elevation) makes and stores aluminum-alloy powders for additive-manufacturing research. A walk-in enclosure inside the lab is supplied with air from a refrigerant (compressor) dehumidifier and exhausted continuously to building exhaust. The surrounding room sits at 21.7-22.2 C and 35-60% relative humidity (RH), dew point 6-13 C, tracking outdoor humidity. On the first night with the dehumidifier on, air inside the enclosure was 24 C at 35-42% RH (dew point 8-10 C) while the room was expected at about 22 C and 56% RH (dew point about 13 C); a hand-held reading showed about 27 C (80 F) at about 30% RH. So the compressor heat raises the enclosure temperature by roughly 2-5 C while the dehumidifier removes about 15-30% of the water vapor. Powders stored there, in sealed containers with silica-gel packets inside chemical storage cabinets, include gas-atomized AlSi10Mg (15-45 um, from MSE Supplies), silicon powder (98-99.5% Si), stainless-steel powder, and soon ultrasonically atomized aluminum alloys containing Mg, Cu, Zn, Li, Sc, Zr, Ce and Er, made in an argon-purged atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder). Question: what do published powder-storage, powder-ageing and powder-reuse studies on laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (and other aluminum AM powders such as AlSi7Mg, Scalmalloy, Al-Cu and Al-Ce alloys) report about oxygen pickup, moisture or hydrogen pickup, flowability (Hall flow, avalanche angle, cohesion) and hydrogen porosity in printed parts after storage at controlled temperature and humidity? Report conditions (temperature, RH, container, duration), measured changes with numbers, and DOIs. Which drying procedures (temperature, time, vacuum) were shown to restore the powder? What storage temperature and RH do aluminum AM powder suppliers (e.g., Valimet, Carpenter Additive, IMR Metal Powder Technologies, ECKART, Oerlikon, EOS, SLM Solutions) and standards or guides (ASTM F3049, ISO/ASTM 52907, ASTM F3318, ASTM F3571 or others) recommend? Finally, what is known about the risks introduced by temperature differences and cycling during storage: condensation when a container stored in a cooler place is opened in warmer humid air or vice versa, pressure-driven air exchange ('breathing') of imperfectly sealed containers, and the reduced water capacity of silica gel at higher temperature? Could silica gel or its dust contaminate aluminum powders stored with it? Give quantitative values with DOIs, and say explicitly where evidence is lacking.

Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.

I'll help you research published studies on aluminum alloy powder storage for additive manufacturing, focusing on AlSi10Mg and related alloys. Let me start by creating a comprehensive plan to address all aspects of your question.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Powder feedstock is the primary input to metal additive manufacturing processes such as laser powder bed fusion. Its characteristics are crucial for producing high-quality components. Realization of the waste reduction and cost benefits that this technology offers requires reclaiming, processing, and reusing powder feedstock. While these benefits can be significant, there are challenges related to the industrial implementation of powder reuse, including the variability in powder quality that can propagate through to the produced material. This variability can be both negative and positive, but ultimately leads to uncertainty for both users and regulators. This means material and process qualifications are difficult to achieve when powder feedstock is being repeatedly reused. This study reports the effects of 175 Ti-6Al-4V ELI powder reuse cycles, characterized at 23, 104, and 175 reuses, in a certified medical device production facility, whereby powder was topped up with virgin powder from the same production lot after each build cycle. To the best of our knowledge, this is the longest reuse campaign reported in the literature. During this campaign, flowability improved with Hall flow rate decreasing by 5.4% and apparent density increasing by 0.8%. The particle size distribution remained stable, with net changes of no more than 2.1%. Particle elongation decreased by 2.9%, and the form factor distribution narrowed around its unchanged mean. Oxygen concentration progressively increased in both the powder (8.2%) and the produced material (25.1%). The average microhardness increased by 3.7% at all measured indentation depths, which is attributed to this oxygen pickup. All property means remained within the material specification limits for both powder and produced material throughout the reuse campaign. The findings of this study suggest that such extensive reuse campaigns can be implemented while fulfilling the requirements of industry powder material specifications, although such reuse processes do induce variability in the properties of both the powder and produced material. The degree of this variability is specific to the type of powder reuse approach implemented and the specific characteristics of the associated powder processing environments.</jats:p>

Abstract:
In this paper, the capability of laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) systems to process stainless steel alloys is reviewed. Several classes of stainless steels are analyzed (i.e., austenitic, martensitic, precipitation hardening and duplex), showing the possibility of satisfactorily processing this class of materials and suggesting an enlargement of the list of alloys that can be manufactured, targeting different applications. In particular, it is reported that stainless steel alloys can be satisfactorily processed, and their mechanical performances allow them to be put into service. Micro surface roughness typical of the as-built material can act as a crack initiator, reducing the strength in both quasi-static and dynamic conditions.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) has attracted significant attention in both the industry and academic fields since its inception, providing unprecedented advantages to fabricate complex-shaped metallic components. The printing quality and performance of L-PBF alloys are influenced by numerous variables consisting of feedstock powders, manufacturing process, and post-treatment. As the starting materials, metallic powders play a critical role in influencing the fabrication cost, printing consistency, and properties. Given their deterministic roles, the present review aims to retrospect the recent progress on metallic powders for L-PBF including characterization, preparation, and reuse. The powder characterization mainly serves for printing consistency while powder preparation and reuse are introduced to reduce the fabrication costs. Various powder characterization and preparation methods are presented in the beginning by analyzing the measurement principles, advantages, and limitations. Subsequently, the effect of powder reuse on the powder characteristics and mechanical performance of L-PBF parts is analyzed, focusing on steels, nickel-based superalloys, titanium and titanium alloys, and aluminum alloys. The evolution trends of powders and L-PBF parts vary depending on specific alloy systems, which makes the proposal of a unified reuse protocol infeasible. Finally, perspectives are presented to cater to the increased applications of L-PBF technologies for future investigations. The present state-of-the-art work can pave the way for the broad industrial applications of L-PBF by enhancing printing consistency and reducing the total costs from the perspective of powders.
