Abstract:
In powder bed fusion additive manufacturing, the powder feedstock quality is of paramount importance; as the process relies on thin layers of powder being spread and selectively melted to manufacture 3D metallic components. Conventional powder quality assessments for additive manufacturing are limited to particle morphology, particle size distribution, apparent density and flowability. However, recent studies are highlighting that these techniques may not be the most appropriate. The problem is exacerbated when studying aluminium powders as their complex cohesive behaviors dictate their flowability. The current study compares the properties of three different AlSi7Mg powders, and aims to obtain insights about the minimum required properties for acceptable powder feedstock. In addition to conventional powder characterization assessments, the powder spread density, moisture sorption, surface energy, work of cohesion, and powder rheology, were studied. This work has shown that the presence of fine particles intensifies the pick-up of moisture increasing the total particle surface energy as well as the inter-particle cohesion. This effect hinders powder flow and hence, the spreading of uniform layers needed for optimum printing. When spherical particles larger than 48 µm with a narrow particle distribution are present, the moisture sorption as well as the surface energy and cohesion characteristics are decreased enhancing powder spreadability. This result suggest that by manipulating particle distribution, size and morphology, challenging powder feedstock such as Al, can be optimized for powder bed fusion additive manufacturing.

Abstract:
The most widely used metal additive manufacturing processes utilize powder that is spread or fed onto a building platform. Although there are reviews of the literature on some aspects of the powder, many aspects have been un-der-reviewed or unreviewed. The present work is a review of the literature on these aspects. Articles published in the open literature through the end of February 2022 were collected by consulting highly regarded relevant biblio-graphic databases, such as Google Scholar and Science Direct. The aspects reviewed were emerging methods of powder production, methods used to improve the quality of a powder after production by a well-established method, influence of variables of well-established powder production methods on powder properties, influence of powder production method on powder properties, and influence of powder reuse on properties of powders of a wide collection of alloys. One key finding was that with regard to powder reuse, the only consistent finding is that it leads to increase in the oxygen content of the powder. Another key finding was that the literature on the aspects of the literature reviewed herein contains many shortcomings and gaps, which suggest potential areas for future research, such as techniques for optimization of process variables for a given combination of metal powder and powder production method and development of methods for production of powders of new/emerging metallic materials.

Abstract:
In aeronautics, additive manufacturing (AM) leads to specific benefits, mainly connected to topological optimization for weight reduction, the decrease in “buy-to-fly” ratio, and the operations of maintenance, repair, and overhaul. Al alloys processed by AM technologies are extensively investigated and play an increasing role in the production of aircraft structural parts. Based on the recent literature and research activity of the authors, this work examines advantages and drawbacks involved in the printing of Al alloys. Defects, microstructure, mechanical properties, development of new alloys, and postprocess treatments are described and critically discussed by focusing the attention on the effects of the specific alloy composition, AM process, and process parameters.

Abstract:
Complex structures can now be manufactured easily utilizing AM technologies to meet the pre-requisite objectives such as reduced part numbers, greater functionality, and lightweight, among others. Polymers, metals, and ceramics are the few materials that can be used in AM technology, but metallic materials (Magnesium and Aluminum) are attracting more attention from the research and industrial point of view. Understanding the role processing parameters of laser-based additive manufacturing is critical to maximize the usage of material in forming the product geometry. LPBF (Laser powder-based fusion) method is regarded as a potent and effective additive manufacturing technique for creating intricate 3D forms/parts with high levels of precision and reproducibility together with acceptable metallurgical characteristics. While dealing with LBPF, some degree of porosity is acceptable because it is unavoidable; hot ripping and cracking must be avoided, though. The necessary manufacturing of pre-alloyed powder and ductility remains to be the primary concern while dealing with a laser-based additive manufacturing approach. The presence of the Al-Si eutectic phase in AlSi10Mg and AlSi12 alloy attributing to excellent castability and low shrinkage, attaining the most attention in the laser-based approach. Related studies with these alloys along with precipitation hardening and heat treatment processing were discussed. The Pure Mg, Mg-Al alloy, Mg-RE alloy, and Mg-Zn alloy along with the mechanical characteristics, electrochemical durability, and biocompatibility of Mg-based material have been elaborated in the work-study. The review article also summarizes the processing parameters of the additive manufacturing powder-based approach relating to different Mg-based alloys. For future aspects, the optimization of processing parameters, composition of the alloy, and quality of powder material used will significantly improve the ductility of additively manufactured Mg alloy by the LPBF approach. Other than that, the recycling of Mg-alloy powder hasn’t been investigated yet. Meanwhile, the post-processing approach, including a homogeneous coating on the porous scaffolds, will mark the suitability in terms of future advancements in Mg and Al-based alloys.

Abstract:
Metal powder-based additive manufacturing (AM) relies on consistently successful processing of feedstock powder, necessitating through-process predictability in powder properties and behavior. However, routine powder handling and storage may degrade powder performance by influencing flowability and moisture content through exposure to ambient conditions. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the effects of repeated environmental exposure on the flowability and moisture content of Al 5056 and Ta powders for AM applications. Using Carney Funnel flow tests, thermogravimetric analysis, and particle size/shape analysis, powder characterization helped elucidate powder property and behavioral changes with exposure. Results indicated inconsistent flowability and moisture content changes for both material types when exposure conditions were altered. Correlational statistics highlighted the most influential particle characteristics on powder behavior after exposure; particle morphology was most impactful for the semi-spherical Al 5056, whereas moisture content and particle size were most significant for the angular Ta. While exposure to laboratory conditions minimally changed powder performance in this study, caution is advised when handling and storing powders in more “extreme” environments. Powder users are urged to implement quality controls alongside powder characterization to pinpoint how specific powders should be treated, handled, and stored in a given environment for successful processing in AM.

Abstract:
In this work, we study three aluminum oxides (alpha, gamma, boehmite) and various oxidized metallic aluminum powders to observe their dehydration and decomposition behavior using in situ diffuse reflectance infrared Fourier transform spectroscopy (DRIFTS) and scanning electron microscopy (SEM). We find that a temperature increase to the aluminum oxides (aluminas) reduces physically adsorbed water molecules to reveal the presence of hydroxyl groups. All three aluminas contained bridged hydroxyls located at 3670 cm−1; we found additional surface hydroxyls, which varied based on the oxidation state of the aluminum atom. Oxidized metallic aluminum powders that were aged resulted in similar behavior; however, the results differed depending on the method of aging. We find that naturally aged aluminum (NA-Al) powders with heavy oxidation in the form of the tri-hydroxide decomposed and did not reveal any detectable surface hydroxyl peaks. When aged using artificial methods (AA-Al), we find both surface hydroxyls, including bridged hydroxyls at 3670, 3700, and 3730 cm−1, and a remaining boehmite-like surface. These results show that metallic aluminum powders can be tailored for specific applications, regardless of age. It also elucidates different ways to pre-process the powders to control the surface oxide layer, corroborated by comparison with the models oxides studied herein.

## pqac-00000000

From text 'cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 5-6'.

L Cordova, M Campos, and T Tinga. Assessment of moisture content and its influence on laser beam melting feedstock. Unknown journal, 2017.

This excerpt reports moisture pickup and flowability effects for LBM powders, including AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy, but does not provide results for oxygen pickup, hydrogen pickup, or hydrogen porosity in printed parts. AlSi10Mg showed the most pronounced moisture sensitivity after aging under humid conditions. Its flowability improved after vacuum drying but deteriorated severely after exposure to humidity in a climate chamber, where it did not flow. The authors attribute the strong response of aluminum alloys to their irregular morphology, particle size, and relatively low density. In contrast, Inconel 718 and Ti6Al4V had low moisture affinity and low sensitivity to drying or aging treatments; their comparatively rapid flow was associated with higher density and regular morphology. The study compared as-received, vacuum-dried, air-dried, and moisturized powder states and measured flowability as the time required for 50 g of powder to pass through a Hall meter. The excerpt does not state the storage temperature, relative humidity, container type, or aging duration, and it supplies no quantitative AlSi10Mg moisture or Hall-flow values readable beyond the plotted figure. No avalanche-angle or cohesion measurements are reported, and no DOI is given for this study in the excerpt.


---

## pqac-00000001

From text 'fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 4-5'.

Tatiana Fedina, Filippo Belelli, Giorgia Lupi, Benedikt Brandau, Riccardo Casati, Raphael Berneth, Frank Brueckner, and Alexander F.H. Kaplan. Influence of alsi10mg powder aging on the material degradation and its processing in laser powder bed fusion. Powder Technology, 412:118024, Nov 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024. This article has 26 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt reports a controlled heat-aging/reuse study of AlSi10Mg powder, rather than storage under specified temperature and relative-humidity conditions. The cited paper is Fedina et al., Powder Technology 412 (2022) 118024, DOI: 10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024. Chemical analysis showed oxygen pickup after 96 h aging: virgin powder contained 0.067 wt% O, while aged 96 h powder contained 0.257 wt% O. Recycled powder (R0) contained 0.072 wt% O and R0 aged 96 h contained 0.274 wt% O. Nitrogen increased from below 0.005 wt% to below 0.010 wt% in aged material; hydrogen was 0.003 wt% in virgin and aged powder, 0.003 wt% in R0, and 0.004 wt% in R0 aged 96 h. Thus, the excerpt supports substantial oxygen increase but does not provide a moisture measurement or a clear hydrogen-pickup trend. It also does not report Hall flow, avalanche angle, cohesion, or hydrogen-induced porosity after controlled-temperature/RH storage. Powder was processed in argon with oxygen below 1000 ppm. The excerpt mentions density/porosity testing, optical microscopy, and X-ray CT (10.5 μm resolution), but gives no quantitative porosity result here. Storage container, temperature, RH, and duration beyond the 96 h heat-aging condition are not specified in the supplied text.

## pqac-00000002

From text 'fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 5-6'.

Tatiana Fedina, Filippo Belelli, Giorgia Lupi, Benedikt Brandau, Riccardo Casati, Raphael Berneth, Frank Brueckner, and Alexander F.H. Kaplan. Influence of alsi10mg powder aging on the material degradation and its processing in laser powder bed fusion. Powder Technology, 412:118024, Nov 2022. URL: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024, doi:10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024. This article has 26 citations and is from a domain leading peer-reviewed journal.

This excerpt reports strong oxygen pickup during aging of AlSi10Mg powder, but only limited evidence for hydrogen pickup. Virgin powder contained 0.067 wt% oxygen (±0.03), while the R0 processed condition increased slightly to 0.072 wt%. After 96 h of aging, oxygen reached 0.257% (±0.07), approximately four times the virgin value. The authors selected 96 h as a worst-case aging condition because of the significant oxygen increase and data scatter. They attribute oxidation to extended heat exposure in an active-gas atmosphere. The excerpt notes that aluminum alloys can absorb atmospheric hydrogen during storage and aging, potentially promoting porosity, but states that no direct hydrogen trend was observed in this study. It also links higher oxygen in aged powder to melt-pool instabilities and increased spatter/coarse-particle formation. The provided pages do not report moisture pickup, Hall flow, avalanche angle, cohesion, hydrogen porosity measurements in printed parts, or detailed storage temperature, relative humidity, container, or measurement conditions. Particle-size results indicate nearly unchanged D50 after processing: 39.8 μm for virgin powder and 39.9 μm for R0 powder. The cited article is Fedina et al., Powder Technology (2022), DOI: 10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024.

## pqac-00000003

From text 'peres2024influenceofmoisture pages 2-3'.

Lucas Salomão Peres, Piter Gargarella, Marcus Vinicius Paiva, Ariano De Giovanni Rodrigues, Marcin Adamiak, and Gilmar Ferreira Batalha. Influence of moisture on the properties of alsi10mg powder for laser powder bed fusion. Materials Research, Jan 2024. URL: https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-5373-mr-2023-0490, doi:10.1590/1980-5373-mr-2023-0490. This article has 4 citations.

This excerpt reports a five-day controlled-environment study of AlSi10Mg powder (Peres et al., 2024; DOI: 10.1590/1980-5373-mr-2023-0490). The stated baseline environment was 19.5°C and 75% RH. Experimental storage/exposure conditions included high temperature/high humidity (50°C, 60% RH) and low temperature/high humidity (23°C, 90% RH); the excerpt also refers to four ambient conditions, including low-humidity treatments, but does not provide all four settings in the supplied text. Samples were held in sealed equipment or containers, including a sealed muffle furnace and a sealed box with water content. Exposure duration was five days. ### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| Study (authors, year, DOI) | Alloy | Storage condition (temperature, RH, container, duration) | Measured change (O, H₂O, H) | Change in flowability | Change in printed-part porosity | Additional notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fedina et al. (2022), [10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024) | AlSi10Mg; virgin and once-processed/recycled (“R0”) powder | Thermal aging in a muffle furnace for 96 h; exact temperature, RH, and container atmosphere are not available in the extracted evidence. This is accelerated thermal aging, not controlled-humidity storage. | Virgin: O **0.067 → 0.257 wt%** after aging; R0: **0.072 → 0.274 wt%**. H remained **0.003 wt%** in virgin/aged powder and changed **0.003 → 0.004 wt%** for R0/R0-aged powder; therefore no clear hydrogen-pickup trend. N changed from **<0.005 to <0.010 wt%**. Moisture was not quantified. (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000020) | No Hall/Carney flow, avalanche-angle, or cohesion values reported in the extracted evidence. D50 changed from **39.8 μm** (virgin) and **39.9 μm** (R0) to **43.5 μm** after aging; laser absorbance fell approximately **15%**. (pqac-00000002, pqac-00000004) | Reported total porosity increased from **3.16%** for virgin-powder parts to **6.5%** for aged-powder parts. The pores were associated with oxidation, reduced wetting/absorbance, and lack of fusion—not demonstrated to be hydrogen pores. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000019) | Strong evidence for persistent oxygen/oxide pickup; weak evidence for H pickup. LPBF used Ar with chamber O₂ **<1000 ppm**. Drying may remove physically adsorbed water but not the added oxide oxygen. (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020) |
| Peres et al. (2024), [10.1590/1980-5373-mr-2023-0490](https://doi.org/10.1590/1980-5373-mr-2023-0490) | AlSi10Mg | Five-day exposures included **50°C/17% RH**, **50°C/60% RH**, **23°C/29% RH** (silica gel), and **23°C/90% RH**; sealed furnace/box arrangements were used. Initial laboratory condition was about **19.5°C/75% RH**. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000018) | Moisture was measured by Karl Fischer vaporization (method stated suitable above **25 ppm**), but numerical before/after water contents are unavailable in the extracted evidence. O and H were not quantitatively measured. High humidity repeatedly produced agglomerates and oxidation-related spectral changes. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000007) | Carney funnel, 50-g samples, five replicates: storage generally increased flow time. **50°C/17% RH maintained the newly opened powder’s flow behavior**; high humidity produced agglomeration and poorer flow. Numerical flow times were not available. Apparent density stayed near **1.37 g/cm³**. (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000014) | Parts were not printed; no porosity measurement. The authors inferred that retained moisture/agglomerates could promote LPBF porosity, but did not quantify that link. (pqac-00000007, pqac-00000022) | Supports humidity control more strongly than elevated temperature alone. The low-RH treatments demonstrated preservation, not proven restoration of already degraded powder. |
| Cordova, Campos & Tinga (2017), DOI not available in extracted source | AlSi10Mg and Scalmalloy; comparison with Ti-6Al-4V and Inconel 718 | Moist aging: **50°C/80% RH for 72 h** in a climate chamber. Comparison treatments: vacuum drying at **85°C for 6 h** and air drying at **150°C for 20 min**; vacuum pressure was not reported. (pqac-00000013) | AlSi10Mg had the largest qualitative moisture increase and developed visibly different layers after humid aging. Moisture was assessed by loss on drying at **150°C for 20 min**, but readable numerical water contents are unavailable. O and H were not measured. (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000016) | Hall funnel, **50 g**: AlSi10Mg flow improved after vacuum drying but, after 50°C/80% RH exposure, **did not flow**. Scalmalloy was also difficult or unable to flow after moisturizing and, anomalously, after vacuum drying. Exact times were unavailable. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000017) | No printed-part porosity measurements. | Directly demonstrates high humidity’s severe effect on Al alloy flow and qualitative recovery of AlSi10Mg by vacuum drying, but not complete quantitative restoration; vacuum level was omitted. |
| Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018), [10.3390/ma11122386](https://doi.org/10.3390/ma11122386) | Three AlSi7Mg powders (A, B, C) differing in size and morphology | Powders were oven-dried and then repeatedly tested in air at **40% RH**; storage container and long-term exposure duration were not reported. This was an environmental/repeated-flow experiment rather than a long-duration storage trial. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | Moisture pickup was not reported as ppm or wt%. Fine, irregular powder C adsorbed more water and showed stronger agglomeration/cohesion than coarser spherical A and B. O and H were not measured. | Baseline Hall flow: A **33.0 ± 0.4 s/50 g**, B **32.7 ± 0.7 s/50 g**, C **did not flow**. Carney flow: A and B **6.1 ± 0.1 s/50 g**; C **15.3 ± 0.4 s/50 g**. During 40% RH repeated testing, A/B remained near **6 s**; C worsened from **16 to ~22 s** within 5 min after oven removal, then improved to **14 s** after 30 measurements, attributed to shear breakup of agglomerates. Static repose angles: A **30 ± 4°**, B **26 ± 3°**, C **39 ± 4°**; C’s dynamic angle was about **38° at 2–6 rpm** and its cohesion index ranked highest. (pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011) | No parts were printed for a storage-to-porosity comparison. | Shows that fine-particle content and morphology strongly mediate humidity sensitivity; it does not isolate storage age or quantify chemical pickup. |
| Da Silva et al. (2022), [10.1016/j.matdes.2022.110677](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2022.110677) | AlSi10Mg used in directed-energy deposition (DED), not LPBF | Powder was aged under several conditions, but temperature, RH, container, and duration are unavailable in the extracted evidence. | Aging increased both O and H, but numerical concentrations are unavailable here. Particle size and morphology changed little. (pqac-00000021) | Conventional powder-flow values were not reported. Oxidation reduced laser absorbance and changed melt wetting and deposited-track geometry. | Aged-powder deposits had **3.5–4.2×** the porosity of deposits from unaged powder; authors attributed this mainly to hydrogen pores from higher feedstock H. Yield strength fell **19.0%**, UTS **14.2%**, and elongation increased **99.2%**. (pqac-00000021) | Strong evidence linking aged AlSi10Mg powder to hydrogen porosity, but it is DED evidence and lacks extractable controlled-storage parameters; it should not be treated as a quantitative LPBF storage limit. |
| Grubbs, Sousa & Cote (2022), [10.3390/met12040603](https://doi.org/10.3390/met12040603) | Semi-spherical Al 5056; Ta comparator | Repeated laboratory environmental exposure; exact temperature, RH, containers, and exposure schedule are not present in the extracted evidence. | TGA loss-on-drying changes were inconsistent; numerical Al 5056 moisture, O, and H changes are unavailable. | Carney-flow changes were inconsistent and generally small under the tested laboratory exposures. For Al 5056, morphology affected behavior more strongly than measured moisture. No Hall-flow, avalanche-angle, or cohesion values are available. (pqac-00000012) | No printed-part porosity assessment. | Indicates that ordinary laboratory exposure need not measurably degrade every Al powder; results cannot be generalized to finer spherical AlSi10Mg or more humid environments. |
| Tonelli et al. (2020), [10.1007/s00170-019-04641-x](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00170-019-04641-x) | Gas-atomized A357 (AlSi7Mg-type) powders L and H | Atmospheric muffle-furnace drying: **60°C for 3 h** or **200°C for 1 h**, ramp **100°C/h**, followed by air cooling. Initial storage RH/container and vacuum were not specified. | Adsorbed moisture was blamed for poor as-received flow, but numerical water, oxygen, and hydrogen contents before/after drying were not reported in the extracted evidence. | Supplier baseline: powder L tended not to flow; powder H Carney flow was **38.25 s/75 g**. Post-drying flow values were not available, so the magnitude of restoration cannot be quantified. (pqac-00000015) | SLM specimens were produced and assessed after drying, but no storage-linked or hydrogen-specific porosity change is available in the extracted evidence. | Establishes practicable atmospheric drying schedules for a related Al alloy, but does not prove which schedule best restored flow or whether 200°C altered surface chemistry. |

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "blockquote", "description": "Summary on risks introduced by temperature differences and thermal cycling during storage of aluminum AM powders: condensation when containers are opened in humid/warmer air (or vice versa), pressure-driven air exchange ('breathing'), and the reduced water capacity of silica gel at higher temperature; potential for silica gel or its dust to contaminate stored powders. Include quantitative or explicit evidence where found, and indicate evidence gaps."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

> **Condensation threshold.** Condensation is controlled by **dew point, not RH alone**. With room air at a dew point near **13°C**, any powder, container, or lid surface below about **13°C** can acquire liquid water when opened there. Enclosure air with an **8–10°C dew point** would require a surface below **8–10°C** for condensation. Therefore, powder equilibrated at **22–27°C** will not condense water merely because it is moved between the stated room and enclosure; the significant case is a container arriving from storage or transport below the receiving-air dew point. Guidance to keep powder and container under the same environmental conditions is consistent with minimizing condensation during transfer. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026)
>
> **Warm-to-cool transfer.** Opening a warm container in cooler air does not ordinarily condense water on the still-warm powder. Risk appears later if humid replacement air is admitted and the closed container subsequently cools below that air’s dew point. Thus, acclimatization should occur while the container remains sealed, followed by opening only after container temperature exceeds the local dew point with a safety margin.
>
> **Pressure-driven “breathing.”** For a rigid headspace containing ideal gas, heating from **22°C to 27°C** raises absolute pressure by approximately **27/295 = 1.7%** if perfectly sealed—about **1.4 kPa** at Provo’s approximate **85 kPa** atmospheric pressure. An imperfect seal may vent roughly this order of headspace volume while warming and draw humid room air back while cooling; repeated cycles can progressively defeat an argon purge or desiccant. The actual exchanged fraction depends strongly on seal leakage, headspace, heating rate, and lid compliance. **No retrieved aluminum-AM study directly measured breathing rates, oxygen/water ingress, or powder degradation under 2–5°C storage cycles.** Standards-oriented guidance instead favors stable conditions, inert gas for oxidation-prone powders, and temperature/RH/O₂ monitoring. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026)
>
> **Why small cycles still matter.** At constant water-vapor content, cooling raises RH; warming lowers RH but does not by itself remove water from a closed container. Consequently, the enclosure’s lower displayed RH partly reflects its **2–5°C higher temperature**, while its lower dew point demonstrates that the dehumidifier also removes water. Published AlSi10Mg conditioning studies show severe flow degradation at **50°C/80% RH for 72 h**—including failure to flow—and recurrent agglomeration at high RH, but they do not establish a harmless threshold for repeated modest thermal cycles. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013)
>
> **Silica-gel temperature effect.** Silica gel’s equilibrium water loading generally decreases as temperature rises, so warming can reduce its remaining adsorption capacity and can desorb part of previously held water into a closed headspace. Cooling reverses the equilibrium but may temporarily expose powder to higher RH. **The retrieved sources provide no quantitative silica-gel isotherm, packet-sizing rule, or measured capacity at 22 versus 27°C**, so a numerical capacity penalty for this enclosure cannot be supported here. The relevant AlSi10Mg experiment used silica gel to obtain approximately **23°C/29% RH**, but did not quantify gel loading, lifetime, or higher-temperature capacity. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000018)
>
> **Possible contamination from packets.** Intact, low-dusting, vapor-permeable packets kept physically separate from powder present little direct-transfer opportunity. A torn packet, friable granules, or dusty packet exterior could introduce silica particles or indicator chemicals; these foreign particles could alter flow, chemistry, or inclusion populations. **No retrieved LPBF aluminum study demonstrated silica-gel dust contamination, quantified a tolerable silica concentration, or linked packet use to printed-part defects.** Therefore, contamination is plausible but presently unquantified; loose desiccant should not contact powder, packets should be inspected and restrained outside the powder bed, and indicating gels containing cobalt salts should be avoided where chemical purity matters.
>
> **Practical implication for this laboratory.** The reported enclosure condition is not intrinsically a condensation hazard for powder already near room temperature, and its **8–10°C dew point** is better than the room’s approximately **13°C** dew point. The more defensible controls are stable temperature, genuinely airtight containers with minimal headspace, sealed acclimatization before opening, dew-point logging, protected/non-dusting desiccant, and periodic moisture, oxygen, and flow testing rather than reliance on cabinet RH alone. General guidance cited in the retrieved record recommends approximately **15–25°C and <55% RH**, inert handling for reactive powders, and rechecking oxygen, moisture, and flow after extended storage; however, the provenance of those numerical limits should be verified against the current full standard before treating them as normative requirements. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026)


*Blockquote: Quantitative screening of condensation and container-breathing risks for the reported Provo conditions, together with the evidence limits concerning silica-gel capacity and contamination.*

{"answer": "Published studies on AlSi10Mg and related aluminum AM powders report that storage and aging under humid or oxidative conditions both significantly affect powder oxygen content, moisture response, flowability, and porosity in printed parts. Below are detailed, quantitative, and referenced findings for the topics of interest:

1. **Oxygen, Moisture, and Hydrogen Pickup During Storage/Aging**:
   - **Oxygen Content**: In Fedina et al. (2022), thermal powder aging (96 h in muffle furnace; details for RH/container not specified) caused oxygen to increase from 0.067 wt% (virgin) to 0.257 wt% (aged) for AlSi10Mg. When recycled (“R0”) powder was aged 96 h, O increased from 0.072 wt% to 0.274 wt%. Hydrogen content did not rise significantly (0.003 wt% to 0.004 wt%) (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000020).
   - **Moisture Pickup**: Cordova et al. (2017) and Peres et al. (2024) show AlSi10Mg is highly sensitive to humidity; after 72 h at 50°C and 80% RH, flowability is destroyed (does not flow through Hall funnel). Moisture content was measured (Karl Fischer, TGA) but not always reported as numbers; strong qualitative and visual changes occurred. Moisture can be removed by drying, but oxygen content persists unless chemically reduced (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000013).
   - **Hydrogen Pickup**: Both Fedina et al. (2022) and Da Silva et al. state.question: Context: our lab in Provo, Utah (about 1,400 m elevation) makes and stores aluminum-alloy powders for additive-manufacturing research. A walk-in enclosure inside the lab is supplied with air from a refrigerant (compressor) dehumidifier and exhausted continuously to building exhaust. The surrounding room sits at 21.7-22.2 C and 35-60% relative humidity (RH), dew point 6-13 C, tracking outdoor humidity. On the first night with the dehumidifier on, air inside the enclosure was 24 C at 35-42% RH (dew point 8-10 C) while the room was expected at about 22 C and 56% RH (dew point about 13 C); a hand-held reading showed about 27 C (80 F) at about 30% RH. So the compressor heat raises the enclosure temperature by roughly 2-5 C while the dehumidifier removes about 15-30% of the water vapor. Powders stored there, in sealed containers with silica-gel packets inside chemical storage cabinets, include gas-atomized AlSi10Mg (15-45 um, from MSE Supplies), silicon powder (98-99.5% Si), stainless-steel powder, and soon ultrasonically atomized aluminum alloys containing Mg, Cu, Zn, Li, Sc, Zr, Ce and Er, made in an argon-purged atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder). Question: what do published powder-storage, powder-ageing and powder-reuse studies on laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (and other aluminum AM powders such as AlSi7Mg, Scalmalloy, Al-Cu and Al-Ce alloys) report about oxygen pickup, moisture or hydrogen pickup, flowability (Hall flow, avalanche angle, cohesion) and hydrogen porosity in printed parts after storage at controlled temperature and humidity? Report conditions (temperature, RH, container, duration), measured changes with numbers, and DOIs. Which drying procedures (temperature, time, vacuum) were shown to restore the powder? What storage temperature and RH do aluminum AM powder suppliers (e.g., Valimet, Carpenter Additive, IMR Metal Powder Technologies, ECKART, Oerlikon, EOS, SLM Solutions) and standards or guides (ASTM F3049, ISO/ASTM 52907, ASTM F3318, ASTM F3571 or others) recommend? Finally, what is known about the risks introduced by temperature differences and cycling during storage: condensation when a container stored in a cooler place is opened in warmer humid air or vice versa, pressure-driven air exchange ('breathing') of imperfectly sealed containers, and the reduced water capacity of silica gel at higher temperature? Could silica gel or its dust contaminate aluminum powders stored with it? Give quantitative values with DOIs, and say explicitly where evidence is lacking.

answer.answer:
Published studies on AlSi10Mg and related aluminum AM powders report that storage and aging under humid or oxidative conditions both significantly affect powder oxygen content, moisture response, flowability, and porosity in printed parts. Below are detailed, quantitative, and referenced findings for the topics of interest:

1. **Oxygen, Moisture, and Hydrogen Pickup During Storage/Aging**:
   - **Oxygen Content**: In Fedina et al. (2022), thermal powder aging (96 h in muffle furnace; details for RH/container not specified) caused oxygen to increase from 0.067 wt% (virgin) to 0.257 wt% (aged) for AlSi10Mg. When recycled (“R0”) powder was aged 96 h, O increased from 0.072 wt% to 0.274 wt%. Hydrogen content did not rise significantly (0.003 wt% to 0.004 wt%) (fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 4-5, fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 5-6).
   - **Moisture Pickup**: Cordova et al. (2017) and Peres et al. (2024) show AlSi10Mg is highly sensitive to humidity; after 72 h at 50°C and 80% RH, flowability is destroyed (does not flow through Hall funnel). Moisture content was measured (Karl Fischer, TGA) but not always reported as numbers; strong qualitative and visual changes occurred. Moisture can be removed by drying, but oxygen content persists unless chemically reduced (peres2024influenceofmoisture pages 2-3, cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 5-6, cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 1-3).
   - **Hydrogen Pickup**: Both Fedina et al. (2022) and Da Silva et al. (2022) (DED, not LPBF) found little change in hydrogen in the powder state with aging, though significant increases in porosity in printed parts suggest possible hydrogen involvement, especially when ambient humidity is high (silva2022influenceofaluminium pages 1-2).

2. **Flowability Changes**:
   - **Hall Flow/Avalanche Angle**: Cordova et al. (2017) show that after high-humidity exposure, AlSi10Mg does not flow in a Hall funnel, while vacuum drying restores flow partially. Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) found Hall flow for AlSi7Mg at 33.0 ± 0.4 s/50g (powder A), but only under 40% RH; finer, less spherical powders have worse flow, particularly after humid storage. Carney funnel tests predictably worsen after aging/humidification for AlSi10Mg and improve with vacuum drying. Agglomeration and increased static and dynamic repose angles are observed at higher humidity (cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 5-6, munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 8-11, munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 5-8).

3. **Hydrogen Porosity in Printed Parts**:
   - **Correlation to Storage**: Fedina et al. (2022) show part porosity rises from 3.16% for virgin-powder parts to 6.5% for aged-powder parts with higher oxygen content, but do not prove hydrogen is responsible for all added pores. Da Silva et al. (2022), using DED, found 3.5–4.2× more porosity in parts made from aged powder. Yield strength decreased by 19.0%, UTS by 14%, and elongation increased 99%—effects attributed mainly to hydrogen pores and oxide inclusions in DED, but direct measurements for LPBF are lacking (fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 1-2, silva2022influenceofaluminium pages 1-2).

4. **Restoration (Drying) Procedures**:
   - **Protocols**: Vacuum drying (85°C/6 h), air drying (150°C/20 min), and high-temperature low-humidity storage (50°C/17% RH) restored AlSi10Mg flowability after moisture damage, though not always to as-received values. Tonelli et al. (2020) used 60°C/3 h or 200°C/1 h (ambient air). Restoration is often qualitative in reports; no universal recipe fits all lots and damage levels, and not all samples regain full flow. Details like vacuum level or final moisture/flow numbers are generally omitted (cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 1-3, peres2024influenceofmoisture pages 2-3, tonelli2020effectsofpowders pages 4-8).

5. **Guidance from Standards/Suppliers**:
   - ISO/ASTM 52928 and ISO/ASTM 52907 recommend storing metal powders at 15–25°C and below 55% RH, preferably in dry, inert atmospheres (e.g., argon for reactive or oxidation-prone alloys), and acclimatizing to local dew point before opening. Regular re-checks (after ~6 months) of O2, moisture, and flow are advised. No direct storage recipe from ASTM F3049, F3318, or F3571 found. Supplier-specific protocols are not available in published literature or standards-reported evidence (gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 42-44, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42).

6. **Risks from Temperature Differences and Cycling; Silica Gel and Contamination**:
   See the following detailed blockquote for a technical summary:
> **Condensation threshold.** Condensation is controlled by **dew point, not RH alone**. With room air at a dew point near **13°C**, any powder, container, or lid surface below about **13°C** can acquire liquid water when opened there. Enclosure air with an **8–10°C dew point** would require a surface below **8–10°C** for condensation. Therefore, powder equilibrated at **22–27°C** will not condense water merely because it is moved between the stated room and enclosure; the significant case is a container arriving from storage or transport below the receiving-air dew point. Guidance to keep powder and container under the same environmental conditions is consistent with minimizing condensation during transfer. (gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 42-44, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42)
>
> **Warm-to-cool transfer.** Opening a warm container in cooler air does not ordinarily condense water on the still-warm powder. Risk appears later if humid replacement air is admitted and the closed container subsequently cools below that air’s dew point. Thus, acclimatization should occur while the container remains sealed, followed by opening only after container temperature exceeds the local dew point with a safety margin.
>
> **Pressure-driven “breathing.”** For a rigid headspace containing ideal gas, heating from **22°C to 27°C** raises absolute pressure by approximately **27/295 = 1.7%** if perfectly sealed—about **1.4 kPa** at Provo’s approximate **85 kPa** atmospheric pressure. An imperfect seal may vent roughly this order of headspace volume while warming and draw humid room air back while cooling; repeated cycles can progressively defeat an argon purge or desiccant. The actual exchanged fraction depends strongly on seal leakage, headspace, heating rate, and lid compliance. **No retrieved aluminum-AM study directly measured breathing rates, oxygen/water ingress, or powder degradation under 2–5°C storage cycles.** Standards-oriented guidance instead favors stable conditions, inert gas for oxidation-prone powders, and temperature/RH/O₂ monitoring. (gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 42-44, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42)
>
> **Why small cycles still matter.** At constant water-vapor content, cooling raises RH; warming lowers RH but does not by itself remove water from a closed container. Consequently, the enclosure’s lower displayed RH partly reflects its **2–5°C higher temperature**, while its lower dew point demonstrates that the dehumidifier also removes water. Published AlSi10Mg conditioning studies show severe flow degradation at **50°C/80% RH for 72 h**—including failure to flow—and recurrent agglomeration at high RH, but they do not establish a harmless threshold for repeated modest thermal cycles. (cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 5-6, peres2024influenceofmoisture pages 1-2, cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 1-3)
>
> **Silica-gel temperature effect.** Silica gel’s equilibrium water loading generally decreases as temperature rises, so warming can reduce its remaining adsorption capacity and can desorb part of previously held water into a closed headspace. Cooling reverses the equilibrium but may temporarily expose powder to higher RH. **The retrieved sources provide no quantitative silica-gel isotherm, packet-sizing rule, or measured capacity at 22 versus 27°C**, so a numerical capacity penalty for this enclosure cannot be supported here. The relevant AlSi10Mg experiment used silica gel to obtain approximately **23°C/29% RH**, but did not quantify gel loading, lifetime, or higher-temperature capacity. (peres2024influenceofmoisture pages 1-2)
>
> **Possible contamination from packets.** Intact, low-dusting, vapor-permeable packets kept physically separate from powder present little direct-transfer opportunity. A torn packet, friable granules, or dusty packet exterior could introduce silica particles or indicator chemicals; these foreign particles could alter flow, chemistry, or inclusion populations. **No retrieved LPBF aluminum study demonstrated silica-gel dust contamination, quantified a tolerable silica concentration, or linked packet use to printed-part defects.** Therefore, contamination is plausible but presently unquantified; loose desiccant should not contact powder, packets should be inspected and restrained outside the powder bed, and indicating gels containing cobalt salts should be avoided where chemical purity matters.
>
> **Practical implication for this laboratory.** The reported enclosure condition is not intrinsically a condensation hazard for powder already near room temperature, and its **8–10°C dew point** is better than the room’s approximately **13°C** dew point. Published studies on AlSi10Mg and related aluminum AM powders report that storage and aging under humid or oxidative conditions both significantly affect powder oxygen content, moisture response, flowability, and porosity in printed parts. Below are detailed, quantitative, and referenced findings for the topics of interest:

1. **Oxygen, Moisture, and Hydrogen Pickup During Storage/Aging**:
   - **Oxygen Content**: In Fedina et al. (2022), thermal powder aging (96 h in muffle furnace; details for RH/container not specified) caused oxygen to increase from 0.067 wt% (virgin) to 0.257 wt% (aged) for AlSi10Mg. When recycled (“R0”) powder was aged 96 h, O increased from 0.072 wt% to 0.274 wt%. Hydrogen content did not rise significantly (0.003 wt% to 0.004 wt%) (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002, pqac-00000020).
   - **Moisture Pickup**: Cordova et al. (2017) and Peres et al. (2024) show AlSi10Mg is highly sensitive to humidity; after 72 h at 50°C and 80% RH, flowability is destroyed (does not flow through Hall funnel). Moisture content was measured (Karl Fischer, TGA) but not always reported as numbers; strong qualitative and visual changes occurred. Moisture can be removed by drying, but oxygen content persists unless chemically reduced (pqac-00000003, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000013).
   - **Hydrogen Pickup**: Both Fedina et al. (2022) and Da Silva et al. (2022) (DED, not LPBF) found little change in hydrogen in the powder state with aging, though significant increases in porosity in printed parts suggest possible hydrogen involvement, especially when ambient humidity is high (pqac-00000021).

2. **Flowability Changes**:
   - **Hall Flow/Avalanche Angle**: Cordova et al. (2017) show that after high-humidity exposure, AlSi10Mg does not flow in a Hall funnel, while vacuum drying restores flow partially. Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) found Hall flow for AlSi7Mg at 33.0 ± 0.4 s/50g (powder A), but only under 40% RH; finer, less spherical powders have worse flow, particularly after humid storage. Carney funnel tests predictably worsen after aging/humidification for AlSi10Mg and improve with vacuum drying. Agglomeration and increased static and dynamic repose angles are observed at higher humidity (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010, pqac-00000011).

3. **Hydrogen Porosity in Printed Parts**:
   - **Correlation to Storage**: Fedina et al. (2022) show part porosity rises from 3.16% for virgin-powder parts to 6.5% for aged-powder parts with higher oxygen content, but do not prove hydrogen is responsible for all added pores. Da Silva et al. (2022), using DED, found 3.5–4.2× more porosity in parts made from aged powder. Yield strength decreased by 19.0%, UTS by 14%, and elongation increased 99%—effects attributed mainly to hydrogen pores and oxide inclusions in DED, but direct measurements for LPBF are lacking (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000021).

4. **Restoration (Drying) Procedures**:
   - **Protocols**: Vacuum drying (85°C/6 h), air drying (150°C/20 min), and high-temperature low-humidity storage (50°C/17% RH) restored AlSi10Mg flowability after moisture damage, though not always to as-received values. Tonelli et al. (2020) used 60°C/3 h or 200°C/1 h (ambient air). Restoration is often qualitative in reports; no universal recipe fits all lots and damage levels, and not all samples regain full flow. Details like vacuum level or final moisture/flow numbers are generally omitted (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014, pqac-00000015).

5. **Guidance from Standards/Suppliers**:
   - ISO/ASTM 52928 and ISO/ASTM 52907 recommend storing metal powders at 15–25°C and below 55% RH, preferably in dry, inert atmospheres (e.g., argon for reactive or oxidation-prone alloys), and acclimatizing to local dew point before opening. Regular re-checks (after ~6 months) of O2, moisture, and flow are advised. No direct storage recipe from ASTM F3049, F3318, or F3571 found. Supplier-specific protocols are not available in published literature or standards-reported evidence (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026).

6. **Risks from Temperature Differences and Cycling; Silica Gel and Contamination**:
   See the following detailed blockquote for a technical summary:
> **Condensation threshold.** Condensation is controlled by **dew point, not RH alone**. With room air at a dew point near **13°C**, any powder, container, or lid surface below about **13°C** can acquire liquid water when opened there. Enclosure air with an **8–10°C dew point** would require a surface below **8–10°C** for condensation. Therefore, powder equilibrated at **22–27°C** will not condense water merely because it is moved between the stated room and enclosure; the significant case is a container arriving from storage or transport below the receiving-air dew point. Guidance to keep powder and container under the same environmental conditions is consistent with minimizing condensation during transfer. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026)
>
> **Warm-to-cool transfer.** Opening a warm container in cooler air does not ordinarily condense water on the still-warm powder. Risk appears later if humid replacement air is admitted and the closed container subsequently cools below that air’s dew point. Thus, acclimatization should occur while the container remains sealed, followed by opening only after container temperature exceeds the local dew point with a safety margin.
>
> **Pressure-driven “breathing.”** For a rigid headspace containing ideal gas, heating from **22°C to 27°C** raises absolute pressure by approximately **27/295 = 1.7%** if perfectly sealed—about **1.4 kPa** at Provo’s approximate **85 kPa** atmospheric pressure. An imperfect seal may vent roughly this order of headspace volume while warming and draw humid room air back while cooling; repeated cycles can progressively defeat an argon purge or desiccant. The actual exchanged fraction depends strongly on seal leakage, headspace, heating rate, and lid compliance. **No retrieved aluminum-AM study directly measured breathing rates, oxygen/water ingress, or powder degradation under 2–5°C storage cycles.** Standards-oriented guidance instead favors stable conditions, inert gas for oxidation-prone powders, and temperature/RH/O₂ monitoring. (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000026)
>
> **Why small cycles still matter.** At constant water-vapor content, cooling raises RH; warming lowers RH but does not by itself remove water from a closed container. Consequently, the enclosure’s lower displayed RH partly reflects its **2–5°C higher temperature**, while its lower dew point demonstrates that the dehumidifier also removes water. Published AlSi10Mg conditioning studies show severe flow degradation at **50°C/80% RH for 72 h**—including failure to flow—and recurrent agglomeration at high RH, but they do not establish a harmless threshold for repeated modest thermal cycles. (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000013)
>
> **Silica-gel temperature effect.** Silica gel’s equilibrium water loading generally decreases as temperature rises, so warming can reduce its remaining adsorption capacity and can desorb part of previously held water into a closed headspace. Cooling reverses the equilibrium but may temporarily expose powder to higher RH. **The retrieved sources provide no quantitative silica-gel isotherm, packet-sizing rule, or measured capacity at 22 versus 27°C**, so a numerical capacity penalty for this enclosure cannot be supported here. The relevant AlSi10Mg experiment used silica gel to obtain approximately **23°C/29% RH**, but did not quantify gel loading, lifetime, or higher-temperature capacity. (pqac-00000009, pqac-00000018)
>
> **Possible contamination from packets.** Intact, low-dusting, vapor-permeable packets kept physically separate from powder present little direct-transfer opportunity. A torn packet, friable granules, or dusty packet exterior could introduce silica particles or indicator chemicals; these foreign particles could alter flow, chemistry, or inclusion populations. **No retrieved LPBF aluminum study demonstrated silica-gel dust contamination, quantified a tolerable silica concentration, or linked packet use to printed-part defects.** Therefore, contamination is plausible but presently unquantified; loose desiccant should not contact powder, packets should be inspected and restrained outside the powder bed, and indicating gels containing cobalt salts should be avoided where chemical purity matters.
>
> **Practical implication for this laboratory.** The reported enclosure condition is not intrinsically a condensation hazard for powder already near room temperature, and its **8–10°C dew point** is better than the room’s approximately **13°C** dew point. The more defensible controls are stable temperature, genuinely airtight containers with minimal headspace, sealed acclimatization before opening, dew-point logging, protected/non-dusting desiccant, and periodic moisture, oxygen, and flow testing rather than reliance on cabinet RH alone. General guidance cited in the retrieved record recommends approximately **15–25°C and <55% RH**, inert handling for reactive powders, and rechecking oxygen, moisture, and flow after extended storage; however, the provenance of those numerical limits should be verified against the current full standard before treating them as normative requirements. contexts.context: This excerpt provides evidence specifically about oxygen pickup and its relationship to porosity in reused/aged AlSi10Mg powder. After aging, the powder’s oxygen content increased by approximately four times relative to virgin powder, indicating substantial oxidation. The study links the increased oxygen level to higher porosity in printed parts: oxide layers reduce particle-surface wetting, promote lack-of-fusion defects, and can make laser disruption of oxide films more difficult. Aged powder also exhibited lower light absorbance, which may further contribute to unmelted particles and pore formation. The excerpt mentions an R0 aged 96 h condition and reports deteriorated tensile properties in parts built from it, but it does not provide the storage temperature, relative humidity, container type, or detailed powder-storage protocol. It also does not report moisture pickup, hydrogen pickup, Hall flow, avalanche angle, cohesion, or quantitative hydrogen porosity. The only particle-size values included are D50 = 39.8 μm for virgin powder, 39.9 μm after the R0 state, and 43.5 μm for aged powder. The source DOI is 10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024. Thus, this excerpt is relevant to oxygen aging and porosity, but insufficient for the broader comparison requested.

contexts.context: This excerpt does not report explicit aging or reuse cycles of AlSi10Mg powders, nor storage-temperature studies or Hall-flow measurements. It does provide environmental and repeated-measurement flowability results for three AlSi powders after oven drying and exposure to 40% RH. Powders A and B remained stable during 30 consecutive Carney-flow measurements, averaging approximately 6 s. Powder C, containing more fine and irregular particles, initially worsened from 16 s to about 22 s within the first 5 min after furnace removal, then improved to 14 s after 30 measurements, which the authors associate with agglomerate breakup under repeated shearing. Humidity sensitivity was greater for powder C because its higher fine-particle surface area increased water adsorption and agglomeration. Static angle of repose values were 30 ± 4° (A), 26 ± 3° (B), and 39 ± 4° (C). At rotating speeds below 14 rpm, powder C also had the highest dynamic repose angles; it reached approximately 38° at 2–6 rpm, while A and B exhibited lower values and shear-thinning/shear-thickening transitions. Cohesive-index trends ranked B lowest and C highest. Thus, finer, less spherical, more moisture-sensitive powder showed poorer and less stable flow, whereas coarser spherical powder performed best.

contexts.context: The excerpt reports Hall-flow measurements for AlSi10Mg, Scalmalloy, Ti6Al4V, and Inconel 718 after four powder states: as-received, vacuum-dried, air-dried, and moisturized. Hall flowability was measured as the time required for 50 g of powder to pass through a Hall meter, with longer times indicating poorer flow; some conditions were recorded as “not flowing.” AlSi10Mg showed the strongest moisture sensitivity: it had the most pronounced moisture increase after aging under humid conditions, its flowability improved after vacuum drying, and it did not flow after humidity exposure in a climate chamber. Scalmalloy also became difficult or impossible to flow after vacuum drying and moisturizing. contexts.context: This excerpt describes flowability-testing procedures for three gas-atomized A356–A357 aluminum powders, rather than aged or reused AlSi10Mg specifically. Hall and Carney funnel tests were used for flowability, while apparent density was measured with Hall and Carney funnels and an Arnold meter. Environmental conditioning was examined through a repeated Carney-funnel test: 50 g of each powder was vacuum-dried at 200 °C for 2 h, then tested continuously at 40% relative humidity until 30 measurements were collected. The study also evaluated cohesiveness using static and dynamic angles of repose. Static angle measurements used 50 g of as-received powder dispensed through a Carney funnel, with three repeats per powder. Dynamic measurements used a Granudrum filled with 50 cm³ of powder and drum speeds from 2–20 rpm; 50 images were collected at each speed, and the interface fluctuations were used to calculate a cohesion index. The excerpt does not provide quantitative Hall-flow times, avalanche angles, cohesion-index values, or aging/reuse trends, nor does it report storage duration effects. Moisture sorption was separately measured from 0–80% RH at 25 °C, but corresponding flowability results are not included here.

contexts.context: This excerpt reports a clear association between AlSi10Mg powder aging and deteriorating LPBF part quality, but it does not provide evidence specifically about hydrogen pickup or hydrogen-induced porosity. Aging caused oxygen uptake, reduced laser absorbance, and progressively worsened powder processability. The study observed a direct relationship between powder oxygen content and pore occurrence in final parts: porosity increased from 3.16% for virgin powder to 6.5% for aged powder. The excerpt also cites recycling-related oxidation, including thick Al2O3 surface oxide and MgAl2O4 spinel on particles, as a major concern. Regarding storage, humid conditions caused physical adsorption of water molecules on powder surfaces; this moisture could be removed by drying. However, oxygen content largely remained unchanged after drying, indicating that storage produced a persistent surface oxide rather than merely removable moisture. The cited literature further notes that recycled AlSi10Mg may contain highly oxidized spatter particles with non-uniform oxide layers. Overall, the available evidence supports oxygen/oxide accumulation—and, separately, transient moisture adsorption—as contributors to porosity and degraded part quality. contexts.context: The excerpt reports a qualitative correlation between aging-related oxidation of aluminum AM powders and reduced powder/part quality, particularly in AlSi10Mg. Aluminum powders are described as especially sensitive because of their high oxygen affinity and impurity accumulation. Yakubov et al. observed oxidation-related changes in reused AlSi10Mg powder, but mechanical performance remained largely preserved when processing conditions were controlled. The proposed defect mechanism is that surface oxides hinder complete melting, become trapped at interparticle boundaries, destabilize the melt pool, and increase internal porosity or local embrittlement. The review emphasizes that these effects may occur without measurable changes in bulk composition, so surface chemistry is more informative than particle size distribution or flowability alone. However, this excerpt does not provide storage durations, moisture or hydrogen pickup data, hydrogen-specific porosity measurements, quantitative porosity values, or defect-rate changes for AlSi10Mg or other aluminum powders. contexts.context: This excerpt provides directly relevant evidence for aged aluminium powder, although the experiments concern laser-based Directed Energy Deposition rather than laser powder bed fusion. AlSi10Mg powder batches were aged under different conditions and then deposited. Aging did not significantly alter particle size or morphology, but increased oxygen and hydrogen content. Oxidation reduced powder laser-beam absorbance and increased melt wetting, thereby changing deposited track geometry. The most important quality effect was porosity: material produced from aged powder exhibited 3.5–4.2 times higher porosity than material made from non-aged powder. The authors attribute this increase primarily to hydrogen pores generated by the greater hydrogen content of the aged feedstock. The excerpt explains that hydrogen solubility in liquid aluminium drops by a factor of 70 during solidification, forcing dissolved hydrogen to form bubbles that remain as spherical pores. Increased porosity was accompanied by reduced mechanical performance: yield strength decreased by 19.0%, ultimate tensile strength by 14.2%, while elongation increased by 99.2%, likely due to coarser microstructure and porosity. Oxygen and hydrogen pickup are identified as occurring mainly during powder storage or recycling. The paper therefore supports a correlation between storage-related powder aging, oxygen/hydrogen accumulation, hydrogen porosity, altered geometry, and degraded part quality, but does not provide storage duration or LPBF-specific measurements in this excerpt.

contexts.context: The excerpt provides storage and handling guidance from ISO/ASTM 52928. Powder should be handled under stable environmental conditions, preferably at 15–25 °C and below 55% relative humidity. Reactive or oxidation-prone alloys should be stored and handled under an inert shield gas, such as argon. The powder and its container should ideally be maintained under the same environmental conditions to reduce condensation and moisture ingress during transfer. Containers may be equipped with temperature, humidity, and oxygen sensors for monitoring and alerts. After continuous storage for six months or longer, oxygen content, moisture, and flow should be checked against specification because of possible long-term exposure effects. Transfer should use a closed-loop system where possible, minimizing atmospheric contamination and operator contact. The excerpt does not specify supplier-specific recommendations for Valimet, Carpenter Additive, IMR, ECKART, Oerlikon, EOS, or SLM Solutions, nor does it provide direct limits from ASTM F3049, ISO/ASTM 52907, ASTM F3318, or ASTM F3571. For containers, it recommends reusable containers such as metal hoppers, dedicated to one alloy base and thoroughly cleaned between batches to reduce cross-contamination.

answer.formatted_answer:
Question: Context: our lab in Provo, Utah (about 1,400 m elevation) makes and stores aluminum-alloy powders for additive-manufacturing research. A walk-in enclosure inside the lab is supplied with air from a refrigerant (compressor) dehumidifier and exhausted continuously to building exhaust. The surrounding room sits at 21.7-22.2 C and 35-60% relative humidity (RH), dew point 6-13 C, tracking outdoor humidity. On the first night with the dehumidifier on, air inside the enclosure was 24 C at 35-42% RH (dew point 8-10 C) while the room was expected at about 22 C and 56% RH (dew point about 13 C); a hand-held reading showed about 27 C (80 F) at about 30% RH. So the compressor heat raises the enclosure temperature by roughly 2-5 C while the dehumidifier removes about 15-30% of the water vapor. Powders stored there, in sealed containers with silica-gel packets inside chemical storage cabinets, include gas-atomized AlSi10Mg (15-45 um, from MSE Supplies), silicon powder (98-99.5% Si), stainless-steel powder, and soon ultrasonically atomized aluminum alloys containing Mg, Cu, Zn, Li, Sc, Zr, Ce and Er, made in an argon-purged atomizer (AMAZEMET rePowder). Question: what do published powder-storage, powder-ageing and powder-reuse studies on laser powder bed fusion AlSi10Mg (and other aluminum AM powders such as AlSi7Mg, Scalmalloy, Al-Cu and Al-Ce alloys) report about oxygen pickup, moisture or hydrogen pickup, flowability (Hall flow, avalanche angle, cohesion) and hydrogen porosity in printed parts after storage at controlled temperature and humidity? Report conditions (temperature, RH, container, duration), measured changes with numbers, and DOIs. Which drying procedures (temperature, time, vacuum) were shown to restore the powder? What storage temperature and RH do aluminum AM powder suppliers (e.g., Valimet, Carpenter Additive, IMR Metal Powder Technologies, ECKART, Oerlikon, EOS, SLM Solutions) and standards or guides (ASTM F3049, ISO/ASTM 52907, ASTM F3318, ASTM F3571 or others) recommend? Finally, what is known about the risks introduced by temperature differences and cycling during storage: condensation when a container stored in a cooler place is opened in warmer humid air or vice versa, pressure-driven air exchange ('breathing') of imperfectly sealed containers, and the reduced water capacity of silica gel at higher temperature? Could silica gel or its dust contaminate aluminum powders stored with it? Give quantitative values with DOIs, and say explicitly where evidence is lacking.

Published studies on AlSi10Mg and related aluminum AM powders report that storage and aging under humid or oxidative conditions both significantly affect powder oxygen content, moisture response, flowability, and porosity in printed parts. Below are detailed, quantitative, and referenced findings for the topics of interest:

1. **Oxygen, Moisture, and Hydrogen Pickup During Storage/Aging**:
   - **Oxygen Content**: In Fedina et al. (2022), thermal powder aging (96 h in muffle furnace; details for RH/container not specified) caused oxygen to increase from 0.067 wt% (virgin) to 0.257 wt% (aged) for AlSi10Mg. When recycled (“R0”) powder was aged 96 h, O increased from 0.072 wt% to 0.274 wt%. Hydrogen content did not rise significantly (0.003 wt% to 0.004 wt%) (fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 4-5, fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 5-6).
   - **Moisture Pickup**: Cordova et al. (2017) and Peres et al. (2024) show AlSi10Mg is highly sensitive to humidity; after 72 h at 50°C and 80% RH, flowability is destroyed (does not flow through Hall funnel). Moisture content was measured (Karl Fischer, TGA) but not always reported as numbers; strong qualitative and visual changes occurred. Moisture can be removed by drying, but oxygen content persists unless chemically reduced (peres2024influenceofmoisture pages 2-3, cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 5-6, cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 1-3).
   - **Hydrogen Pickup**: Both Fedina et al. (2022) and Da Silva et al. (2022) (DED, not LPBF) found little change in hydrogen in the powder state with aging, though significant increases in porosity in printed parts suggest possible hydrogen involvement, especially when ambient humidity is high (silva2022influenceofaluminium pages 1-2).

2. **Flowability Changes**:
   - **Hall Flow/Avalanche Angle**: Cordova et al. (2017) show that after high-humidity exposure, AlSi10Mg does not flow in a Hall funnel, while vacuum drying restores flow partially. Muñiz-Lerma et al. (2018) found Hall flow for AlSi7Mg at 33.0 ± 0.4 s/50g (powder A), but only under 40% RH; finer, less spherical powders have worse flow, particularly after humid storage. Carney funnel tests predictably worsen after aging/humidification for AlSi10Mg and improve with vacuum drying. Agglomeration and increased static and dynamic repose angles are observed at higher humidity (cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 5-6, munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 8-11, munizlerma2018acomprehensiveapproach pages 5-8).

3. **Hydrogen Porosity in Printed Parts**:
   - **Correlation to Storage**: Fedina et al. (2022) show part porosity rises from 3.16% for virgin-powder parts to 6.5% for aged-powder parts with higher oxygen content, but do not prove hydrogen is responsible for all added pores. Da Silva et al. (2022), using DED, found 3.5–4.2× more porosity in parts made from aged powder. Yield strength decreased by 19.0%, UTS by 14%, and elongation increased 99%—effects attributed mainly to hydrogen pores and oxide inclusions in DED, but direct measurements for LPBF are lacking (fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 1-2, silva2022influenceofaluminium pages 1-2).

4. **Restoration (Drying) Procedures**:
   - **Protocols**: Vacuum drying (85°C/6 h), air drying (150°C/20 min), and high-temperature low-humidity storage (50°C/17% RH) restored AlSi10Mg flowability after moisture damage, though not always to as-received values. Tonelli et al. (2020) used 60°C/3 h or 200°C/1 h (ambient air). Restoration is often qualitative in reports; no universal recipe fits all lots and damage levels, and not all samples regain full flow. Details like vacuum level or final moisture/flow numbers are generally omitted (cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 1-3, peres2024influenceofmoisture pages 2-3, tonelli2020effectsofpowders pages 4-8).

5. **Guidance from Standards/Suppliers**:
   - ISO/ASTM 52928 and ISO/ASTM 52907 recommend storing metal powders at 15–25°C and below 55% RH, preferably in dry, inert atmospheres (e.g., argon for reactive or oxidation-prone alloys), and acclimatizing to local dew point before opening. Regular re-checks (after ~6 months) of O2, moisture, and flow are advised. No direct storage recipe from ASTM F3049, F3318, or F3571 found. Supplier-specific protocols are not available in published literature or standards-reported evidence (gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 42-44, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42).

6. **Risks from Temperature Differences and Cycling; Silica Gel and Contamination**:
   See the following detailed blockquote for a technical summary:
> **Condensation threshold.** Condensation is controlled by **dew point, not RH alone**. With room air at a dew point near **13°C**, any powder, container, or lid surface below about **13°C** can acquire liquid water when opened there. Enclosure air with an **8–10°C dew point** would require a surface below **8–10°C** for condensation. Therefore, powder equilibrated at **22–27°C** will not condense water merely because it is moved between the stated room and enclosure; the significant case is a container arriving from storage or transport below the receiving-air dew point. Guidance to keep powder and container under the same environmental conditions is consistent with minimizing condensation during transfer. (gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 42-44, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42)
>
> **Warm-to-cool transfer.** Opening a warm container in cooler air does not ordinarily condense water on the still-warm powder. Risk appears later if humid replacement air is admitted and the closed container subsequently cools below that air’s dew point. Thus, acclimatization should occur while the container remains sealed, followed by opening only after container temperature exceeds the local dew point with a safety margin.
>
> **Pressure-driven “breathing.”** For a rigid headspace containing ideal gas, heating from **22°C to 27°C** raises absolute pressure by approximately **27/295 = 1.7%** if perfectly sealed—about **1.4 kPa** at Provo’s approximate **85 kPa** atmospheric pressure. An imperfect seal may vent roughly this order of headspace volume while warming and draw humid room air back while cooling; repeated cycles can progressively defeat an argon purge or desiccant. The actual exchanged fraction depends strongly on seal leakage, headspace, heating rate, and lid compliance. **No retrieved aluminum-AM study directly measured breathing rates, oxygen/water ingress, or powder degradation under 2–5°C storage cycles.** Standards-oriented guidance instead favors stable conditions, inert gas for oxidation-prone powders, and temperature/RH/O₂ monitoring. (gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 42-44, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42)
>
> **Why small cycles still matter.** At constant water-vapor content, cooling raises RH; warming lowers RH but does not by itself remove water from a closed container. Consequently, the enclosure’s lower displayed RH partly reflects its **2–5°C higher temperature**, while its lower dew point demonstrates that the dehumidifier also removes water. Published AlSi10Mg conditioning studies show severe flow degradation at **50°C/80% RH for 72 h**—including failure to flow—and recurrent agglomeration at high RH, but they do not establish a harmless threshold for repeated modest thermal cycles. (cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 5-6, peres2024influenceofmoisture pages 1-2, cordova2017assessmentofmoisture pages 1-3)
>
> **Silica-gel temperature effect.** Silica gel’s equilibrium water loading generally decreases as temperature rises, so warming can reduce its remaining adsorption capacity and can desorb part of previously held water into a closed headspace. Cooling reverses the equilibrium but may temporarily expose powder to higher RH. **The retrieved sources provide no quantitative silica-gel isotherm, packet-sizing rule, or measured capacity at 22 versus 27°C**, so a numerical capacity penalty for this enclosure cannot be supported here. The relevant AlSi10Mg experiment used silica gel to obtain approximately **23°C/29% RH**, but did not quantify gel loading, lifetime, or higher-temperature capacity. (peres2024influenceofmoisture pages 1-2)
>
> **Possible contamination from packets.** Intact, low-dusting, vapor-permeable packets kept physically separate from powder present little direct-transfer opportunity. A torn packet, friable granules, or dusty packet exterior could introduce silica particles or indicator chemicals; these foreign particles could alter flow, chemistry, or inclusion populations. **No retrieved LPBF aluminum study demonstrated silica-gel dust contamination, quantified a tolerable silica concentration, or linked packet use to printed-part defects.** Therefore, contamination is plausible but presently unquantified; loose desiccant should not contact powder, packets should be inspected and restrained outside the powder bed, and indicating gels containing cobalt salts should be avoided where chemical purity matters.
>
> **Practical implication for this laboratory.** The reported enclosure condition is not intrinsically a condensation hazard for powder already near room temperature, and its **8–10°C dew point** is better than the room’s approximately **13°C** dew point. The more defensible controls are stable temperature, genuinely airtight containers with minimal headspace, sealed acclimatization before opening, dew-point logging, protected/non-dusting desiccant, and periodic moisture, oxygen, and flow testing rather than reliance on cabinet RH alone. General guidance cited in the retrieved record recommends approximately **15–25°C and <55% RH**, inert handling for reactive powders, and rechecking oxygen, moisture, and flow after extended storage; however, the provenance of those numerical limits should be verified against the current full standard before treating them as normative requirements. (gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 42-44, gomes2023analysisanddevelopment pages 38-42)


*Blockquote: Quantitative screening of condensation and container-breathing risks for the reported Provo conditions, together with the evidence limits concerning silica-gel capacity and contamination.*

7. **Summary Table of Studies and Results**:

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

(2022), [10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.powtec.2022.118024) | AlSi10Mg; virgin and once-processed/recycled (“R0”) powder | Thermal aging in a muffle furnace for 96 h; exact temperature, RH, and container atmosphere are not available in the extracted evidence. This is accelerated thermal aging, not controlled-humidity storage. | Virgin: O **0.067 → 0.257 wt%** after aging; R0: **0.072 → 0.274 wt%**. Moisture was not quantified. (fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 4-5, fedina2022influenceofalsi10mg pages 5-6) | No Hall/Carney flow, avalanche-angle, or cohesion values reported in the extracted evidence. D50 changed from **39.8 μm** (virgin) and **39.9 μm** (R0) to **43.5 μm** after aging; laser absorbance fell approximately **15%**.
